      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Mulla Ahmed, who wrote in Persian (translating the Rajatarangini into Persian under the name Bahr-ul-Asman)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d2bfc339-5d8a-4eac-b0eb-755fd259a167",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Another important work in Persian was Tarikh-e-Kashmir by Haider Malik, which means History of Kashmir. Additionally, Abul Fazal's Akbar Nama and Ain-e-Akbari provide information about the history, geography, administration, antiquities, arts, and industries of Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "462c5a90-7d56-479a-8b2b-d21dc902392f",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Accounts of Foreign Travellers",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c8961ddc-3543-465f-a98c-39221487570a",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Several foreign travelers visited the valley and recorded their observations:",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "075ae2b7-2c42-486c-a5c3-4447fb888d45",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Hiuen Tsang: Visited the valley in AD 631 and recorded the conversion of the people to Buddhism by Majjhantika.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "58f9ea83-43cb-4121-8729-53856a8977e6",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Ou-Kong: Visited Kashmir in the middle of the 8th century AD. He described Kashmir as a kingdom surrounded by mountains on all sides and detailed the routes crossing the mountains to Tibet in the East, Baltistan in the North, and Gandhara in the West.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2e53f631-c8b6-4f90-97a4-195e44b2836c",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Alberuni: His work Kitab-ul-Hind gives an accurate account of the valley, confirming Sanskrit sources of the period regarding the people, manners, arts, and crafts of Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e7537aef-4a03-47f6-96d7-9387893966fe",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "European Travellers: Included Father Jerome Xavier (who accompanied Emperor Akbar), Francis Bernier (who visited with Aurangzeb), Desideri, George Forester, Vigne, Drew, Lawrence, and Cunningham. The latter three visited Kashmir after the valley came under Dogra rule and British suzerainty.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2047aae4-1c3f-4024-9373-f323af33dfe8",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME 'KASHMIR'",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b9da8381-43bf-4f2a-a6c1-0c4fb74ee488",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Etymological Theories",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a8ce4831-0cf7-49d8-a58e-118606babb63",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "There are two primary explanations for the origin of the name Kashmir:",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d94a8b1f-f8a1-4690-b18e-d44a3c9363bb",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Kashyap-Mar or Kashyap-Pura: According to legend, the valley was named after the sage Kashyap.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "acea0a5e-9d19-4adf-88a6-176858e92148",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Ka + Shimeera: Derived from 'Ka' meaning water and 'Shimeera' meaning to desiccate. Thus, the name signifies a land that emerged after the desiccation of water.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "365f3462-eb76-483d-86ed-392fdb5c7319",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Earlier Names of Kashmir",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "945a4cd4-c7cc-4ed3-a7f2-f40d8ed81ecb",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Kasperia: The name used by the ancient Greeks.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7e01b7b4-99dd-4113-8b5a-4265e14eae74",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Kashi-Mi-Lo: The name recorded by the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "9d7ce9e2-ca31-48f7-8c27-627c78c9051b",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Kasheer: The traditional name used by the local people of Kashmir themselves.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a3e8d048-7a0e-4e5e-99ce-661115df15d2",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "PREHISTORIC AND EARLY HISTORY",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "12348ad6-509d-49b6-8edd-06f0fbab15cc",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Burzahom — The Neolithic Age",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "0b8461be-d5cf-43f0-8b09-21ad46a71126",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Burzahom was the first Neolithic site to be discovered in Kashmir, located between the banks of Dal Lake and the Zabarvan Hills. At Burzahom, homes were pits dug below ground level using stone tools. The inhabitants made simple grey or reddish-brown handmade pots in different shapes and sizes.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4cfe8049-0cc0-49dc-a8a2-6369e83bc2a4",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Many burials belonging to this phase were discovered, showing that red ochre was smeared on the bodies before burial. Scientists have identified seeds of both wild and cultivated types, including wheat, barley, and different kinds of lentils at the Neolithic levels of Burzahom.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f69acefd-7867-4376-9bde-b4571643e374",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Mahabharata Period",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "9ff29059-ae13-4178-bf94-489021d7f6e3",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The rudiments of the earliest history of Kashmir can be traced to the epic Mahabharata period. According to Mahabharata evidence, the Kambojas ruled over the region during epic times and had a Republican System of Government, with Rajapura (modern Rajouri) as their capital city.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5a4557b8-bc04-4709-a392-472a1c786033",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Later, the Panchalas are believed to have established their sway over the region. The name Peer Panjal is considered a distorted form of the Sanskrit tribal term Panchala. In the Rajatarangini, Kalhana started the history of Kashmir just before the great Mahabharata War. The first king mentioned by him was Gonanda I, who was killed in battle. At the commencement of the Mahabharata War, Gonanda II was ruling Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "29157389-c9f1-405c-8160-34e85589423c",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "After his death, the records of 35 kings who ruled the valley could not be traced because they had been destroyed. However, modern scholar Peer Zada Hassan gave a brief record of these kings from a Persian work by Mulla Ahmed composed during the time of Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin, who obtained the names from an earlier Sanskrit work called Ratnakar.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f2c72d0e-637c-4f92-8642-55f4f1b17d24",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "ANCIENT DYNASTIES AND EMPIRES",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "07d67c2b-20f2-4e6f-a151-3da5608b4e5d",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Mauryan Empire",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "0068cbdb-118a-4490-ad85-f5831c82febd",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Mauryan rule was established over the region of Jammu and Kashmir around the 3rd century BC. The great Mauryan Emperor Ashoka is recorded as having ruled Kashmir. Kalhana mentions that the king was a follower of Buddhism.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ec445c1f-aff1-4b19-ae2f-922504116580",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Ashoka founded the old city of Srinagar, which was then called Purandhistan (or Puranadhisthana). He built many viharas and temples, and repaired an old shrine. At Vijeshwari (modern Bijbehara), he built a Shiva temple, winning the support of the local population who were mostly worshippers of Lord Shiva.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c6eba348-8981-48f5-b0ae-f414f118be58",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Majjhantika, a celebrated Buddhist missionary, was deputed to Kashmir and Urvasa to preach Buddhism. Hiuen Tsang mentions the arrival of 500 monks in Kashmir and Ashoka making a gift of the valley to the Sangha. After the death of Ashoka, his son Jaluka ascended the throne of Kashmir, who was later succeeded by his son King Damodara II. Jaluka was described as a great king who cleared the valley of oppressive Mlechhas (foreign or unclean tribes).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "359464a9-0dd8-4b27-92f8-c599219efe30",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Kushan Empire",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8690dacc-907d-44fb-ac55-d5f521ff9215",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Kalhana's account of the Turushka kings indicates the occupation of the valley by the Kushanas. The three kings mentioned by him were Hushka, Jushka, and Kanishka. Each of them is credited with founding a town named after himself: Hushkapura, Jushkapura, and Kanishkapura. The Kushan kings also built many temples and viharas.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "50d48082-78ac-4c0f-ae3f-1ad7e0b9a2cc",
      "type": "CALLOUT",
      "calloutType": "DEFINITION",
      "title": "The Fourth Buddhist Council",
      "content": "According to many scholars, Kanishka held the Fourth Great Buddhist Council at Kundalvan, identified with Harwan near Shalimar Garden. The historical division of Buddhism into two sects, Hinayana and Mahayana, took place in connection with this council. A learned Kashmir Brahmin named Vasumitra presided over the session, which was attended by nearly 500 Buddhist and Hindu scholars, including Ashvaghosh, Nagarjuna, Vasubandhu, Sungamitra, and Jinamitra."
    },
    {
      "id": "49d142a6-c776-48f7-a89a-2822a212d3be",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Karkota Dynasty",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "3df45730-1721-4660-887c-6d071ab97ad8",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Karkota Dynasty was founded by Durlabhavardhana (AD 625–661). During his reign, the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang visited Kashmir, entering through a huge stone gate at Baramulla. At that time, the entry of all outsiders except Hindus was banned, but Hiuen Tsang received a royal reception and stayed for nearly two years to study Sanskrit and Hindu scriptures.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "041fbad9-101d-4ce4-8da3-c77c56f126c9",
      "type": "HEADING_4",
      "text": "Lalitaditya Muktapida (AD 724–761)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7ceeba08-d8b1-40d2-912a-5fadca82576f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Karkota dynasty gave Kashmir one of its greatest rulers, Lalitaditya Muktapida, often described as the Samudra Gupta of Kashmir. He had an unquenchable desire for world conquest and invaded and conquered many countries in Asia and India, including Punjab, Kannauj, Tibet, Ladakh, Badakshan, Iran, Bihar, Gauda (Bengal), Kalinga (Orissa), South India, Gujarat, Malwa, Marwar, and Sindh. He finally broke the power of the Arabs in Sindh.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "add15dfc-8a93-4896-8062-d33d3a3a7b4b",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Lalitaditya was also a great builder. He built his capital near the sacred shrine of Kheer Bhawani and named it Parihaspur (meaning city of pleasure). Throughout the valley, he built many fine and massive temples. The world-famous Sun Temple of Martand, built on Mattan Karewa, remains a testament to the grandeur of his reign. Alberuni mentions that Kashmiris observed the second of Chaitra as a day of victory to celebrate Lalitaditya's conquests.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c67ca924-1f80-456b-8882-c7d747c8e148",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "MEDIEVAL PERIOD AND DYNASTIES",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "61c08622-6af7-46ad-bc06-2be296a82582",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Utpala Dynasty",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "364c4965-f298-4a66-979f-994d9859035f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Around AD 855–856, Karkota rule ended and the Utpala dynasty assumed power. The most important ruler of this dynasty was Maharaja Avantivarman, who recovered Kashmir from political and economic disorder. His reign witnessed a period of peace, consolidation, and prosperity.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6a739af2-9f9a-4d63-9b26-f7f6b6425a65",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Avantivarman founded his capital city of Avantipur, embellishing it with two temples, one dedicated to Shiva and the other to Vishnu. He was succeeded by his son Shankarvarman, under whom the decline of the Utpala dynasty began.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "aa37f279-ea81-4e24-8247-103876a9806c",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "During the time of King Yasakara (AD 939–948), a Math (hospice) was built for students from India who came to Kashmir for study and meditation, revealing intimate cultural contacts between the valley and the plains of India.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d564b2aa-0166-4398-8197-fecc4d0856c6",
      "type": "HEADING_4",
      "text": "Queen Didda",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a8ee5402-4237-41e4-b7a3-74269c469b96",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "In AD 950, Kshemgupta ascended the throne. He married Princess Didda, daughter of the ruler of Lohara (Poonch) and granddaughter of the Shahi King of Kabul. Queen Didda was the de facto ruler due to her dominating personality. She built many temples and monasteries, including one reserved for people from Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Central India.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "528a5b8b-c947-4794-b72f-636415616ad6",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "In AD 980, Didda formally ascended the throne. Despite her controversial personal life, she was an able and firm ruler. She died in AD 1003, transmitting the throne to her nephew Sangramraj, the son of her brother Udaraj (ruler of Lohara).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "49e0b70b-0f63-480c-8ec1-9413759eb128",
      "type": "CALLOUT",
      "calloutType": "IMPORTANT",
      "title": "Invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni",
      "content": "During Queen Didda's era, Mahmud of Ghazni twice attempted to capture the valley. However, the fort of Lohara, remarkable for its height and strength, proved impregnable, forcing the Sultan to abandon his conquest."
    },
    {
      "id": "992398a2-f398-4519-92be-ba75b12c5357",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Lohara Dynasty",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "929d37d2-a54a-40c6-830d-f5824a7ccc92",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Lohara dynasty, centred at Loharan, was founded by Sangramraj after the death of Queen Didda. It ruled Kashmir for more than a century until the end of Hindu rule. Notable rulers included King Harsha (AD 1089–1101) and King Jaisimha (AD 1128–1155), the last great ruler of the Hindu period, during whose reign Kalhana completed the Rajatarangini. The last ruler of the Lohara dynasty was Vanitadeva, who ruled in AD 1171.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5e2880f1-9610-4dcc-ac01-36f52ef97d22",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Deva Dynasty and Foreign Invasion",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a416707a-e0c1-448c-a110-b6674105e5bf",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Deva dynasty ruled Kashmir from AD 1171 to 1339, with Sangramdev and Sahdev being notable kings. During the reign of Sahdev, Kashmir was invaded by a fierce Mongol\/Tartar chief named Dulucha from Central Asia.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e5f18495-1383-492b-9e19-bc4e2a30e1ff",
      "type": "HEADING_4",
      "text": "Dulucha's Invasion",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "bb120f31-9ff4-4b72-a35f-46ad54bd891b",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "In the beginning of the 14th century, Dulucha invaded the valley through the northern side via Zoji La Pass with an army of about 60,000 men. He carried sword and fire, destroyed towns and villages, and slaughtered thousands. His savage attack practically ended Hindu rule in Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "3f5defa8-6d41-4aa5-9a39-b54f887ef7a9",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "During Sahdev's reign, three adventurers arrived in Kashmir and played a notable role in its political history: Shah Mir from Swat, Rinchen from Ladakh, and Lankar Chak from the Dard territory of Gilgit. All three were granted Jagirs by the King. Rinchen became the ruler of Kashmir for three years, Shah Mir founded the Shah Miri dynasty, and the descendants of Lankar Chak established Chak rule.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "783ddeab-0637-4d37-8022-18c17fc4f0df",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "MUSLIM RULE IN KASHMIR",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "969b4416-9d7e-4f97-a84d-66293f632230",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Shah Miri Dynasty",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e0bda70e-810c-4c6a-ae74-ea4b08a8ff03",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "After the death of Queen Kota, Shah Mir ascended the throne under the name of Sultan Shams-ud-din, founding the Shah Miri dynasty.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "756e4b34-0aaf-4148-9a75-243d0e4786e3",
      "type": "HEADING_4",
      "text": "Sultan Shihab-ud-din (AD 1354–1373)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "bbf86154-31ca-4479-bb5e-1a54be3d6747",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Sultan Shihab-ud-din was full of energy and vigour. He established his sway over neighbouring countries with an army consisting of Damars, Lavans, and hill tribes of Poonch, Rajouri, and Kishtwar. He defeated the ruler of Sindh, the Afghans at Peshawar, and conquered Kabul, Swat, Multan, Badakhshan, and Gilgit.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "faa83e24-0749-4acb-bf25-f7d825df927f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "He also marched towards Delhi and conquered Kangra. His forces were opposed by Feroz Shah Tughlaq on the banks of the Sutlej; the battle was indecisive, leading to a peace treaty where all territory from Sindh to Kashmir was agreed to belong to Kashmir. He founded the town of Shihab-ud-din-pura (modern Shadipur) and has been called the Lalitaditya of medieval Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "fe20e1a0-333d-4813-bce4-bd7ad5d2293b",
      "type": "HEADING_4",
      "text": "Sultan Qutb-ud-din and Sultan Sikandar",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6d283ae0-c992-440b-874f-71c503165694",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "During the reign of Sultan Qutb-ud-din, the famous saint Syed Ali Hamdani visited Kashmir, bringing 700 Syeds from Hamdan who established missionary centres. Qutb-ud-din was succeeded in 1389 by his eldest son, Sultan Sikandar, during whose reign the political atmosphere became highly disturbed.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6f7a6e41-2f97-4906-824a-8b0f8b1c5ec9",
      "type": "HEADING_4",
      "text": "Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (AD 1420–1470)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7e46372d-39d2-4b13-9126-62eb325b58f7",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Shahi-Khan, or Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (popularly known as Budshah), ascended the throne in AD 1420. He reconquered Punjab, Western Tibet, Ladakh, Balti region, Kulu, and Ohind (Hazara). He maintained friendly relations with foreign rulers, exchanging gifts with the Sheriff of Mecca and the kings of Egypt, Gwalior, Sindh, Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, and Delhi.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2f439945-52ff-456d-b21a-62f8eb9cc1bb",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "His administration was marked by several key achievements:",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "03700ccb-b732-4b36-864f-870decf29678",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Agriculture: Dug many canals, reclaiming large areas for cultivation, making Kashmir self-sufficient in food and lowering the price of rice.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "0f45beb6-65ab-4afe-96fe-aaf7bf3187c4",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Religious Tolerance: Allowed complete freedom of worship, recalled Hindus who had fled, permitted forcibly converted Hindus to return to their faith, banned cow slaughter, rebuilt temples at state expense, and almost completely abolished Jaziya.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "60475e21-4bff-424a-b226-c62f0df20606",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Patronage of Letters: Supported Persian and Sanskrit scholars, established a translation department to translate works from Sanskrit into Persian and Arabic, and opened schools and hostels.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e6429499-5082-48c7-ae5d-476d53e27130",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Public Works: Founded the towns of Nowshader, Zainapur, Zainakut, and Zainagir, and built the first wooden bridge at Srinagar, known as Zainakadal.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "21ec2a70-ba13-4a9d-bda9-bf2d15455d66",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "His death in AD 1470 sounded the death knell of the Shah Miri dynasty.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d2fd37c0-b8ea-4858-a3e0-76d854eda003",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Chak Dynasty (AD 1561–1587)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "25c04b2a-1de2-4c7a-9142-40895734b800",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The last Shah Miri ruler, Sultan Habib Shah, was deposed by Gazi Chak, a direct descendant of Lankar Chak. The Chaks, originally Dards from the Gilgit-Hunza area, successfully thwarted early attempts by Mughal Emperors Babur and Humayun to annex Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "1e5c8bc0-442a-46e2-b9b2-f905d2a9f2bc",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Yusuf Shah Chak married the famous poetess Habba Khatoon and developed Gulmarg and Sonamarg as holiday resorts. He was eventually defeated by Akbar's forces under Qasim at Haripura, and died in prison in Bihar, paving the way for Mughal rule in AD 1587.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b64791ae-d2fe-4047-92f8-c6ecaf93958d",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "THE MUGHAL, AFGHAN, AND SIKH PERIODS",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f6cb56cb-b726-4982-a405-f62d509fb534",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Mughal Dynasty (AD 1586–1751)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "30a72ccb-0cf1-4ff7-9241-573b5d58739f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Mughals brought peace and orderly government to Kashmir. Key emperors made significant contributions:",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "931adf85-1844-4571-9cc6-297ca2c448d6",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Akbar: Visited Kashmir three times. His minister Raja Todar Mal made a revenue settlement that forms the basis of modern land settlements. Akbar built the town of Nagar-Magar near Hariparbat and constructed the massive wall around the hill.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c7ddd09b-d71c-441e-973e-0f42eae20490",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Jahangir: Laid out the world-famous Shalimar, Nishat, Achabal, and Verinag gardens.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "049dc431-6ffb-4fcb-94e3-d090e5c03db3",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Shah Jahan: Laid out the Chashmashahi garden and built a portion of Shalimar.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b1a87305-c8cc-4bc6-b078-1eb3c836dd49",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Aurangzeb: Visited only once in AD 1665. His reign marked the beginning of administrative decline and lawlessness.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ba3c813a-25cf-4167-aeaf-36510c37cb3c",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Following the invasion of Nadir Shah, Mughal misrule became intolerable. In AD 1752, Kashmiri noblemen Mir Muqim Kant and Khwaja Zahir Didmari requested Ahmed Shah Abdali of Kabul to bring Kashmir under his control.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f9bc8fb9-16f6-4296-b304-f70f18648386",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Afghan Rule (AD 1762–1819)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "49f0fbbb-f700-436c-bc93-f51a19fdb981",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Ahmed Shah Abdali dispatched an army under Abdullah Khan Ishik Agasi to occupy the valley. The Afghan rule lasted for about sixty-seven years and was characterized as highly despotic and tyrannical. They ruled through various governors and deputies, including Nur-ud-din Khan Bamzai and Buland Khan Bamzai.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "23aafae6-d0c2-47cc-95bf-e51b789a4795",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Sikh Rule (AD 1819–1846)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4e219699-a0e8-4c82-8dcb-b72d4cd6b054",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "To end Afghan tyranny, a Kashmiri deputation led by Pandit Birbal Dhar and his son Pandit Rajak Dhar escaped the valley (aided by Abdul Qadoos, Malik Zulfiqar, and Malik Kamgar) and requested Maharaja Ranjit Singh of Lahore to conquer Kashmir. In AD 1819, Ranjit Singh's army of 30,000 soldiers defeated the Pathans. Sikh rule lasted for twenty-seven years.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4bb431fe-10af-4cae-b960-8355fca3fede",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "THE MODERN PERIOD: DOGRA RULE (AD 1846–1950)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b21f67c6-51db-446e-b369-a75255621e97",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Establishment of Dogra Rule",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "96ffc032-2195-4c09-8c21-c731bf005f7d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "In AD 1846, following the defeat of the Sikhs in the First Anglo-Sikh War, the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh of Jammu for ₹75 lakh under the Treaty of Amritsar. Maharaja Gulab Singh formally entered Srinagar on 9th November 1848. The Dogra rulers claimed descent from the ancient Suryavanshi Kshatriya race.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "63686592-5749-464f-bc7f-87269d840e07",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Dogra Monarchs and Administration",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2da9ea48-43cc-4486-a829-1b66272651e8",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Maharaja Gulab Singh (AD 1846–1857): A ruler of great vigour and determination. He crushed the Galwan plunderers, broke the power of the rebellious Bambas and Khokhas, and built numerous garrisoned forts. He systematically conquered Bhimbar, Rajauri, Skardu, Ram Nagar, Basoli, Bhadarwah, Kishtwar, Astor, Gilgit, Chitral, Yasin, Hunza, Nagar, and Punial.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "934691a1-02c1-4d60-919e-0eb41ab95679",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Maharaja Ranbir Singh (AD 1857–1885): Succeeded Gulab Singh and established a sound administrative system.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a00ab1b9-dc6a-4b55-81fd-85006915ffa5",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Maharaja Hari Singh (AD 1925–1950): Nephew of Maharaja Pratap Singh, he ascended the throne in 1925 and governed the state until his rule ended in 1950.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,

    {
      "id": "00499451-67e3-409f-be72-c7a0c4efbad7",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 1. INTRODUCTION AND SOURCES OF KASHMIR HISTORY",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "cba55350-8227-4db3-a577-e2e2e98d2207",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "There are several ways of reconstructing the past of Kashmir. Kashmiris, who distinguished themselves in many branches of Sanskrit learning, were also meticulous historians who left an almost continuous written record of the valley's history. These histories are supplemented by archeological, numismatic, and foreign accounts.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b66d0c9c-3451-493b-a444-ea95d6dbade3",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Primary Historical Sources\n* **Written Records:** Comprehensive court chronicles, religious texts, and dynastic biographies.\n* **Archaeological Evidence:** Excavations of ancient cities, temples, and megalithic sites.\n* **Numismatic Evidence:** Ancient coins providing chronological markers and economic indicators.\n* **Foreign Accounts:** Travelogues of Chinese pilgrims, Tibetan scholars, Mughal chroniclers, and European explorers.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "65953e71-f1e0-41ed-bbb5-68512f3e93ba",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Sanskrit and Early Chronicles\n* **Kalhana and the Rajatarangini:** Written by the 12th-century poet-historian Kalhana between AD 1148 and 1149, the *Rajatarangini* (The River of Kings) is a landmark historical chronicle. Written in Sanskrit, it contains valuable political, social, and cultural information. Kalhana consulted eleven earlier chronicles, most of which are now lost, to construct his narrative.\n* **The Nilamat Purana:** The earliest known text of Kashmir. It contains sacred legends regarding the origin of the valley and details the religious rites, festivals, and worship ceremonies prescribed by Nila, the Lord of the Kashmir Nagas.\n* **Haracharitachintamani:** Authored by Jayadratha, this text deals specifically with sacred sites, pilgrimages, and local Shaivite traditions.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d7dbacf8-a58c-407b-8e77-faf8e07caf7c",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Muslim Period Chronicles\nDuring the Muslim period, Persian replaced Sanskrit as the language of the court. However, rulers like Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin actively patronized scholars of both languages and commissioned updates to the historical record:\n* **Jonaraja:** A Sanskrit chronicler who brought the *Rajatarangini* up to date. His work, the *Dvitiya Rajatarangini* (Second Rajatarangini \/ *Rajavali*), covers the reigns of late Hindu rulers from Jayasimha to Queen Didda.\n* **Mulla Ahmad:** A Persian scholar who translated Kalhana’s *Rajatarangini* into Persian under the title *Bahr-ul-Asman* (The Ocean of Activity) at the behest of Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin.\n* **Malik Haider:** Wrote the *Tarikh-i-Kashmir* (History of Kashmir) in Persian, providing a valuable internal perspective on the transition to Mughal rule.\n* **Mughal Imperial Records:** Abul Fazl’s *Akbarnama* and *Ain-e-Akbari* offer highly detailed assessments of Kashmir’s revenue system, geography, administration, crafts, and arts following its integration into the Mughal Empire.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "41fe3c55-6176-460e-9261-abefc054ccde",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Accounts of Foreign Travellers\n* **Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang):** Visited the valley in AD 631 during the Karkota dynasty. He entered through the stone gate at Baramulla and recorded the historical conversion of Kashmiris to Buddhism by the missionary Majjhantika.\n* **Ou-Kong:** Visited Kashmir in the middle of the 8th century AD. He described Kashmir as a secure kingdom enclosed by a ring of mountains and mapped out mountain routes leading to Tibet (East), Baltistan (North), and Gandhara (West).\n* **Alberuni:** In his treatise *Kitab-ul-Hind*, he gave an accurate account of the valley's geography, customs, and isolationist policies, confirming contemporaneous Sanskrit records.\n* **European Travellers:** \n  * **Father Jerome Xavier:** Accompanied Emperor Akbar to the valley.\n  * **Francois Bernier:** Visited during the reign of Aurangzeb (AD 1665).\n  * **Later Observers:** Desideri, George Forester, G.T. Vigne, Frederic Drew, Sir Walter Lawrence, and Alexander Cunningham visited Kashmir during the Dogra and British periods, leaving comprehensive records of the state's geography, flora, and administration.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"

    {

    {
      "id": "4aebe584-c829-429e-9933-9f0695c28e76",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "| Book Title | Author \/ Translator | Key Subject Matter |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **Nilamat Purana** | Unknown | Earliest text; sacred legends, rituals, and Naga lore. |\n| **Rajatarangini (Sanskrit)** | Kalhana | Dynastic history of Kashmir up to the 12th century. |\n| **Rajatarangini (Persian)** | Mulla Ahmad | Persian translation commissioned by Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (*Bahr-ul-Asman*). |\n| **Rajatarangini (English)** | M.A. Stein | Definitive translation with critical notes and geographical identifications. |\n| **Rajatarangini (Kashmiri)** | Dr. Bashar Basheer | Kashmiri translation of the 1st, 2nd, and 8th parts of the chronicle. |\n| **Twarikh-i-Kashmir** | Malik Haider | Medieval Persian chronicle written during the Mughal transition. |\n| **Waqt-e-Kashmir** | Khawaja Mohammad | Historical development and administrative structures of the valley. |\n| **Muktasar Tarikh-i-Kashmir** | Birbal Kachru | Concise Persian account of the socio-political shifts in Kashmir. |\n| **Tarikh-i-Hassan** | Pir Hassan Shah | Highly regarded, multi-volume history of Kashmir's dynasties. |\n| **Zaffar Nama** | Sharif-ud-din Yazdi | Detailed military history of Central Asia, Timur, and interactions with Kashmir. |\n| **Valley of Kashmir** | Sir Walter Lawrence | Extensive land settlement records, socioeconomic analysis, and folklore. |\n| **Land of Lamas** | Alexander Cunningham | Geographical and cultural study of Ladakh, Baltistan, and surrounding areas. |\n| **Aatish-i-Chinar** | Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah | Autobiography of Sheikh Abdullah; details modern political movements. |\n| **Rajdarshani** | Ganesh Das Vadhera | History of the Jammu principality and the early Dogra chiefs. |\n| **Tawarikh-i-Jammu** | Hashmatullah Khan | Comprehensive administrative and dynastic history of the Jammu region. |\n| **Twarikh-i-Kishtwar** | Sheoji Dhar | Local chronicle detailing the history, rulers, and culture of Kishtwar. |\n| **Land of Hills** | G. C. Smith | Geographic and topographic accounts of the outer Western Himalayas. |\n| **Gulabnama (Persian)** | Diwan Kirpa Ram | Official court biography of the first Dogra Maharaja, Gulab Singh. |\n| **Gulabnama (English)** | Dr. S. S. Charak | English translation of Diwan Kirpa Ram’s court biography. |\n| **Akbarnama** | Abul Fazl | Mughal imperial chronicle detailing Akbar's annexation of Kashmir. |\n| **Twarikh-i-Dogra** | Narsingh Dass | Dynastic accounts and cultural heritage of the Dogra community. |\n| **Rise and Fall of Jammu Kingdom** | Dr. S. S. Charak | Modern analytical history of the political evolution of Jammu. |",

    {
      "id": "9816f8d1-a84a-46c7-b885-60c74d56f876",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 2. THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME 'KASHMIR'",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "59d206eb-822c-4670-9180-df7d47e90f41",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Etymological Theories\n1. **Kashyap-Mar or Kashyap-Pura:** According to sacred Puranic legend, the valley of Kashmir was originally a vast lake known as *Satisar* (the lake of Sati). The sage **Kashyap** drained the lake at Baramulla (Varahamula) by cutting through the mountain wall, killing the demon Jalodbhava. The reclaimed land was named *Kashyap-Mar* or *Kashyap-Pura* in his honor.\n2. **Ka + Shimeera:** Derived from the Sanskrit words **'Ka'** (water) and **'Shimeera'** (to desiccate\/dry up). The name translates literally to *\"a land desiccated or reclaimed from water.\"*",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e208c5b0-9980-4122-ba09-5340da3ca31d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Historical Names of Kashmir\n* **Kasperia:** The name used by ancient Greek geographers, including Ptolemy.\n* **Kashi-Mi-Lo:** The phonetic name recorded by the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang in his travelogues.\n* **Kasheer:** The traditional, colloquial name used by the native Kashmiri population.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,

    {
      "id": "592555e4-10a7-49c4-98be-310b8609ebb1",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 3. PREHISTORIC AND EARLY HISTORY",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",

      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f1a0c355-405a-4415-ae31-525a51d0798b",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### Burzahom — The Neolithic Age (c. 3000 BC – 1000 BC)\nLocated between the banks of Dal Lake and the Zabarwan Hills, **Burzahom** was the first Neolithic site discovered in Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f31260e1-af91-4dd8-a79b-1bad95bb7820",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Pit-Dwellings:** The early inhabitants lived in circular or oval pits dug deep into the lacustrine soil (Karewas) using stone tools. These pits were plastered with mud and featured wooden post-holes, indicating thatched roofs designed to protect against harsh winters.\n* **Material Culture:** Inhabitants produced coarse gray, black, or reddish-brown handmade pottery. Tools were fashioned from polished stones and animal bones.\n* **Burial Practices:** Burials uncovered at the site show that red ochre was smeared on human skeletons before interment. Domesticated animals (such as dogs and wolves) were also buried alongside their masters.\n* **Agriculture:** Paleo-botanical analysis indicates early cultivation of wheat, barley, and various types of lentils alongside wild plant gathering.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "dba50a62-986b-4a21-b697-11379c4b9366",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Mahabharata Period\nThe earliest dynastic memory of Kashmir is linked to the epic *Mahabharata*. \n* **The Kambojas:** Ancient texts indicate that the Kamboja tribe ruled the region with their republican system of government centered at **Rajapura** (modern **Rajouri**).\n* **The Panchalas:** Later, the Panchalas established their influence over the area. The name **Peer Panjal** is widely considered a linguistic evolution of the ancient Sanskrit tribal term *Panchala*.\n* **Gonandic Dynasty:** Kalhana begins the historical record of *Rajatarangini* just before the Mahabharata War. The first king mentioned is **Gonanda I**, who was killed in battle at Mathura. At the outbreak of the war, his infant successor **Gonanda II** was ruling Kashmir.\n* **The Lost Kings:** Kalhana records that the histories of 35 early kings were lost. However, the 19th-century historian **Peerzada Ghulam Hassan** recovered details of these rulers from a Persian manuscript written by Mulla Ahmad, who had translated an older, lost Sanskrit work called *Ratnakar*.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },

      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 4. ANCIENT DYNASTIES AND EMPIRES",

    {
      "id": "bc6a5f63-b706-441d-b6a9-2b11a3b5ccb0",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Mauryan Empire (c. 322 BC – 185 BC)\nMauryan hegemony was established over Jammu and Kashmir in the 3rd century BC under **Emperor Ashoka**.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "00668711-01b5-498f-b7b4-0ee2560be2a7",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "```\n[Majjhantika's Mission] ──> Deputed by Ashoka ──> Preached Buddhism in Kashmir ──> 500 Monks Arrive\n```",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,

      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e5ed453a-03be-4538-91ed-189d843ddee9",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Srinagar (Pandrethan):** Ashoka founded the original city of Srinagar, known as **Puranadhisthana** (located at modern-day Pandrethan).\n* **Religious Patronage:** Although a patron of Buddhism, Ashoka built several Viharas and also patronized local Shaivism, building a grand Shiva temple at **Bijbehara** (ancient *Vijeshwari*).\n* **Succession:** After Ashoka’s death, his son **Jaluka** ascended the throne. Jaluka cleared the valley of foreign invader tribes (Mlechhas) and was succeeded by his son, **Damodara II**.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "dad9ad39-4b54-4035-86b9-c072807dcaba",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Kushan Empire\nKalhana’s *Rajatarangini* details the occupation of the valley by three Turushka (Kushan) kings: **Hushka**, **Jushka**, and **Kanishka**. \n* **Town Foundations:** Each king founded a town named after himself: *Hushkapura* (Ushkur, Baramulla), *Jushkapura* (Zukur, Srinagar), and *Kanishkapura* (Kanispora, Baramulla).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "24249133-8eea-4584-811e-54ce92c3e53a",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> **The Fourth Buddhist Council (c. 1st Century AD)**\n> Held under the patronage of **Emperor Kanishka** at **Kundalvan** (identified as Harwan near Shalimar Garden, Srinagar). \n> * **Presidency:** Presided over by the Kashmiri scholar **Vasumitra**, with **Ashvaghosh** serving as vice-president.\n> * **Significance:** Attended by 500 Buddhist and Hindu scholars (including Nagarjuna and Vasubandhu). The council finalized the separation of Buddhism into the **Hinayana** and **Mahayana** sects.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7f86d724-8955-446b-aa5c-8003483adba7",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "---",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "96c60ee2-06a0-457a-81cb-3d9b660cbcfa",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Karkota Dynasty (c. AD 625 – 855)\nFounded by **Durlabhavardhana** (AD 625–661), the Karkota dynasty (also known as the **Nagas**) turned Kashmir into a major regional power.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2db4bae8-eff0-43b9-892e-e8929ea36b0f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Foreign Visits:** Both Chinese pilgrims **Hiuen Tsang** and **Ou-Kong** visited Kashmir during this dynasty. Hiuen Tsang spent two years (AD 631–633) studying Sanskrit scriptures, entering through the stone gate at Baramulla.\n* **Lalitaditya Muktapida (AD 724–761):** Known as the **\"Samudra Gupta of Kashmir,\"** Lalitaditya was a military genius. He launched successful military campaigns across Asia and India, conquering Punjab, Kannauj, Tibet, Ladakh, Bihar, Bengal, Gujarat, and parts of Southern India. He also repelled the Arab forces in Sindh.\n* **Martand Sun Temple:** Built by Lalitaditya on the Mattan Karewa, this temple is a masterpiece of early medieval temple architecture. He also built a grand capital called **Parihaspur** (City of Pleasure) near the Kheer Bhawani shrine.\n* **Jayapida:** The grandson of Lalitaditya, **Jayapida** (Vinayaditya), was the last prominent ruler of this dynasty, known for his patronage of literature and arts.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5b10cbcc-c53d-4a6f-853b-c1ab606a9128",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "```\n       [KARKOTA EMPIRE BUILDERS]\n       Durlabhavardhana (Founder; Visited by Hiuen Tsang)\n                │\n       Lalitaditya Muktapida (Conqueror; Built Martand Sun Temple & Parihaspur)\n                │\n       Jayapida (Last powerful ruler; patron of letters)\n```",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },

      "isBold": false,

    {
      "id": "77c66a9e-43f7-479a-812e-5dcfe1ec910f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 5. MEDIEVAL PERIOD AND DYNASTIES",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c553d9ba-734a-4b33-bf30-6ec651cdd99a",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Utpala Dynasty (c. AD 855 – 939)\nIn AD 855, the Karkota dynasty was succeeded by the Utpala dynasty, founded by **Avantivarman**.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "faeac731-61c8-488b-8e3f-6b77666c25ce",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Avantivarman (AD 855–883):** Brought an era of peace, stability, and agricultural recovery. He founded the capital **Avantipur** and built two majestic temples: *Avantisvara* (dedicated to Shiva) and *Avantisvamin* (dedicated to Vishnu).\n* **Suyya’s Engineering Feats:** Avantivarman’s chief engineer, **Suyya**, engineered a massive flood-control scheme. He regulated the course of the Jhelum river, cleared silt blockages at the mouth of the Wular Lake, and reclaimed large tracts of swampy land for agriculture. He founded the town of **Suyyapura** (modern **Sopore**).\n* **Shankarvarman (AD 883–902):** Succeeded Avantivarman, marking the start of the dynasty's decline. He founded **Shankarpura** (modern **Pattan**). To finance his military campaigns, he imposed heavy taxes and introduced the system of **Begar** (forced labor).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8f6b0c60-8c71-4833-af9e-e4f975d297d3",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Gupta Dynasty (c. AD 948 – 1003)\nThe Gupta Dynasty was founded by **Parva Gupta**. His son **Kshemgupta** ascended the throne in AD 950.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e443bfad-7e1a-4494-9953-1d3fba5a145b",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Queen Didda:** Kshemgupta married Princess **Didda**, the daughter of the King of Lohara (Poonch) and granddaughter of the Hindu Shahi King of Kabul. A highly ambitious, intelligent, and forceful figure, Didda ruled through puppet kings before formally ascending the throne in AD 980. She built several temples and monasteries.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d558487e-d9a9-46d5-9482-3449489d11ac",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> **Invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni**\n> During Queen Didda's era, Mahmud of Ghazni twice attempted to invade and capture Kashmir. Both times, his forces were stopped by the impregnable defenses of the **Loharakot Fort** (located in modern Poonch), forcing him to retreat.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "20dbe256-65a1-4535-bb7d-1801befcfa6d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Lohara Dynasty (c. AD 1003 – 1171)\nFounded by **Sangramraj** (Queen Didda's nephew) after her death in AD 1003.\n* **King Harsha (AD 1089–1101):** An eccentric, highly cultured ruler who was also a patron of arts, but whose heavy taxation and destruction of temple idols for gold earned him the title of an iconoclast in his later years.\n* **King Jaisimha (AD 1128–1155):** The last great ruler of the Hindu period. It was during his reign that Kalhana completed the *Rajatarangini*. The dynasty ended with the rule of **Vanitadeva** in AD 1171.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b3f6897d-8ae3-4c94-9ef9-49767002c80f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Deva Dynasty and Mongol Invasion (c. AD 1171 – 1339)\nThe Deva dynasty ruled Kashmir until the final collapse of Hindu political power in the early 14th century.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "3eea7891-4b93-4fb3-bc07-f61a41c491d3",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Dulucha’s Invasion:** During the reign of **King Sahdev**, a ruthless Mongol commander named **Dulucha** (or Zulju) invaded Kashmir through the Zoji La pass with a cavalry of 60,000 men. Dulucha pillaged the valley, slaughtered the male population, and enslaved thousands. Sahdev fled to Kishtwar, leaving the administrative apparatus in collapse.\n* **The Three Adventurers:** Sahdev's reign saw the arrival of three foreign adventurers who shaped Kashmir's history:\n  1. **Shah Mir** (from Swat, Pakistan)\n  2. **Rinchen** (a Buddhist prince from Ladakh)\n  3. **Lankar Chak** (a Dard chief from Gilgit)\n* **Rinchen's Rule:** Following Dulucha's withdrawal, **Rinchen** seized the throne and ruled for three years (AD 1320–1323). He converted to Islam under the influence of the Sufi saint **Sayyid Sharf-ud-din** (popularly known as Bulbul Shah), adopting the name **Sultan Sadr-ud-din**. He was Kashmir's first Muslim ruler.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "878e43cf-3499-40ad-99ca-faba3d89cdd8",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "---",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "dca0262e-b272-444c-96f7-32564dad21c6",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 6. MUSLIM RULE IN KASHMIR",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "16172673-f380-41db-b01d-d7a23374ecc3",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Shah Miri Dynasty (c. AD 1339 – 1561)\nFollowing the death of Queen Kota Deva (the last Hindu ruler), **Shah Mir** ascended the throne in AD 1339 under the name **Sultan Shams-ud-din**, founding the Shah Miri Dynasty.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "fe2f652f-e28f-4a76-9aef-f1734517d871",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Sultan Shihab-ud-din (AD 1354–1373):** Often called the **\"Lalitaditya of Medieval Kashmir,\"** he was a capable military general. He expanded the boundaries of Kashmir to include Kabul, Gilgit, Baltistan, Ladakh, and Kishtwar. He fought Feroz Shah Tughlaq on the banks of the Sutlej River, leading to a treaty that recognized Kashmarian authority over territories from Sindh to Kashmir. He founded **Shihab-ud-din-pura** (modern Shadipur).\n* **Sultan Sikandar (AD 1389–1413):** Popularly referred to by some chroniclers as the **\"Aurangzeb of Kashmir.\"** He banned social customs like the **Sati system** and music. During his reign, Central Asian invader **Taimur (Timur)** sent envoys to Kashmir, presenting Sikandar with a **wooden elephant** as a diplomatic gift.\n* **Sufi Missions:** During the reign of Sultan Qutb-ud-din, the celebrated Sufi saint **Mir Sayyid Ali Hamdani** (Shah-i-Hamdan) arrived in Kashmir with 700 Syeds from Hamdan, Iran. This mission introduced Islamic jurisprudence, central Asian crafts, and the weaving of Kani shawls.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d35592e0-003d-4651-aa28-c56da30cd61d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "```\n                  [SULTAN ZAIN-UL-ABIDIN (\"BUDSHAH\")]\n                  ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐\n        Socio-Economic Reforms                 Patronage & Culture\n   - Recalled exiled Pandits              - Biographies: *Zain Prakashan* & *Zain Charit*\n   - Abolished Jaziya & Sati ban          - Introduced Paper Mache from Samarkand\n   - Built Zainakadal (1st wooden bridge)  - Jonaraja wrote *Dvitiya Rajatarangini*\n```",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e3e8d124-e6c9-4ba9-9dc1-2b610dfb50ca",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (AD 1420–1470):** Affectionately called **\"Budshah\"** (The Great King). \n  * **Social & Religious Reforms:** He initiated an era of religious harmony. He recalled Kashmiri Pandits who had fled, allowed forcibly converted Hindus to return to their faith, banned cow slaughter, rebuilt damaged temples, and abolished the Jaziya tax.\n  * **Art and Craft:** He introduced the art of **Paper Mache** and silk weaving, bringing master craftsmen from Samarkand.\n  * **Public Works:** He founded the towns of Nowshahr, Zainapur, Zainakot, and Zainagir. He also built **Zainakadal**, the first wooden bridge in Srinagar.\n  * **Biographies:** His life was documented in two major contemporary works: *Zain Prakashan* by Yodh Bhatt and *Zain Charit* by Pandit Nathuram.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "670fe4dd-4b46-423c-bcad-270cbbad4550",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Chak Dynasty (AD 1561–1587)\nThe Shah Miri dynasty ended when **Gazi Chak** (a descendant of Lankar Chak) deposed Sultan Habib Shah. The Chaks were originally Dardic warriors from the Gilgit-Hunza region.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5348d25c-624e-4737-933b-4704f284d9fb",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Mughal Defiance:** The Chaks repeatedly repulsed annexation attempts by the Mughal Emperors Babur and Humayun.\n* **Yusuf Shah Chak:** A patron of arts who married the legendary peasant-poetess **Habba Khatoon** (known as the *Nightingale of Kashmir*). He developed Gulmarg and Sonamarg into health resorts. He was eventually lured into negotiations, arrested by Akbar's general Qasim Khan at Haripura, and imprisoned in Bihar where he died. This paved the way for Mughal annexation in AD 1587.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ae25c447-e32a-496e-bceb-b7f00d4c4992",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "---",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "72c7736a-083c-4b11-b978-97ede985e69f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "## 7. THE MUGHAL, AFGHAN, AND SIKH PERIODS",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ec2ea76e-ce7f-4d22-8895-45f8d57e167a",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Mughal Dynasty (AD 1586 – 1751)\nFollowing the capture of Yusuf Shah Chak, Akbar integrated Kashmir into the Kabul Subah of the Mughal Empire.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e077d430-334e-429f-8a54-247688f44e7d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Emperor Akbar:** Visited Kashmir three times. His finance minister, **Raja Todar Mal**, carried out a comprehensive land revenue settlement. Akbar built the fortified town of **Nagar-Magar** around the Hari Parbat hill and constructed its outer stone wall (*Kalai*).\n* **Emperor Jahangir:** Deeply enamored by the valley's beauty, he visited frequently and laid out the world-famous gardens of **Shalimar**, **Nishat**, **Achabal**, and **Verinag**.\n* **Emperor Shah Jahan:** Developed the **Chashma Shahi** garden and expanded Jahangir's pavilions at Shalimar.\n* **Emperor Aurangzeb:** Visited only once in AD 1665. Following his death, Mughal authority weakened, leading to administrative decline and local uprisings.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f9c3c375-7364-4c35-b4c3-47113b0359e6",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Afghan Rule (AD 1753 – 1819)\nFaced with administrative decline, Kashmiri noblemen Mir Muqim Kanth and Khwaja Zahir Didmari invited the Durrani ruler of Kabul, **Ahmad Shah Abdali**, to take control of the valley. Afghan rule lasted for **67 years**, during which Kabul appointed **28 Governors (Subedars)**.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d4531de3-1de6-4b13-82b2-ae1802319ffa",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Character of Rule:** Generally remembered as an era of high taxation and administrative instability.\n* **Amir Khan (Afghan Governor):** Constructed the **Sher Garhi Fort** (which served as the seat of government) and **Amira Kadal** (bridge). He also dug the **Amir Khan Nallah**, a canal connecting Anchar Lake to Dal Lake.\n* **Atta Mohammad Khan:** The only Afghan governor to focus on restoring peace. He declared independence from Kabul and issued currency coins stamped with the name of Kashmir’s patron saint, **Sheikh Nur-ud-din Rishi (RA)** (Nund Rishi).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2cd0f6f8-2d33-4eb7-957a-189e87d9ede3",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "---",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "335d808c-7f49-4d93-b902-5f360f1a42fd",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "### The Sikh Rule (AD 1819 – 1846)\nTo end Afghan misrule, a Kashmiri delegation led by **Pandit Birbal Dhar** and his son Rajak Dhar escaped the valley. Assisted by local chiefs, they traveled to Lahore to petition **Maharaja Ranjit Singh** to conquer Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "73831ff9-1075-44dd-80e7-2608dd1ec9a4",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "```\n[Birbal Dhar's Mission] ──> Petitions Ranjit Singh ──> Battle of Shopian (1819) ──> Sikh Rule Begins\n```",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "36c00096-d9c8-4d6c-856b-1352efa4e184",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "* **Battle of Shopian (5 July 1819):** Maharaja Ranjit Singh's Sikh army defeated the Afghan forces led by Jabbar Khan, ending Durrani rule in Kashmir.\n* **Sikh Administration:** The Sikhs ruled Kashmir for 27 years through **10 Governors**:\n  * **First Governor:** Diwan Moti Ram\n  * **Last Governor:** Sheikh Imam-ud-din\n  * **Most Capable Governor:** Colonel Mian Singh (Colonel Sahib), who stabilized the economy after the Great Famine of 1833.\n* **General Zorawar Singh:** In 1834, the general of the Jammu principality (under Sikh suzerainty), **Wazir Zorawar Singh**, launched military campaigns that conquered **Ladakh**, **Zanskar**, and **Baltistan**, extending the state's borders to the trans-Himalayan region.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "69f9600b-5b62-445f-875f-0eafaf12c756",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "---",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
