    },
    {
      "id": "f7c7c4ef-5418-40a4-9dea-4f0664b7785e",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "2. THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME 'KASHMIR'",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "edd0674a-0d33-402e-b316-9edb08bc68a6",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Etymological Theories",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4ef69197-cc97-48c8-9aec-17322ac3fea8",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Kashyap-Mar or Kashyap-Pura: According to sacred Puranic legend, the valley of Kashmir was originally a vast lake known as Satisar (the lake of Sati). The sage Kashyap drained the lake at Baramulla (Varahamula) by cutting through the mountain wall, killing the demon Jalodbhava. The reclaimed land was named Kashyap-Mar or Kashyap-Pura in his honor.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "975ff2fe-f1c6-4b71-a091-452b9f9053ee",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Ka + Shimeera: Derived from the Sanskrit words 'Ka' (water) and 'Shimeera' (to desiccate\/dry up). The name translates literally to \"a land desiccated or reclaimed from water.\"",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "2711ef24-b0bf-43e8-8eee-f36f2a9c188f",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Historical Names of Kashmir",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "818aaf7e-11ee-4d2d-8126-65f46cbdce4c",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Kasperia: The name used by ancient Greek geographers, including Ptolemy.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "782d4af6-1480-46c6-acb2-ebe5e6cca761",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Kashi-Mi-Lo: The phonetic name recorded by the Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang in his travelogues.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5c908199-a582-4c37-bcf7-f72cd07599f0",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Kasheer: The traditional, colloquial name used by the native Kashmiri population.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "1819d166-ec8a-474a-8943-33ce9fba2f53",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "3. PREHISTORIC AND EARLY HISTORY",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "cc245564-0193-4a27-bd0a-955cd93d36ee",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Burzahom — The Neolithic Age (c. 3000 BC – 1000 BC)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "466a3d0c-a82d-420f-b964-dedf199d678c",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Located between the banks of Dal Lake and the Zabarwan Hills, Burzahom was the first Neolithic site discovered in Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "99cb36e3-2733-4f40-b3fe-44bb3d12f100",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Pit-Dwellings: The early inhabitants lived in circular or oval pits dug deep into the lacustrine soil (Karewas) using stone tools. These pits were plastered with mud and featured wooden post-holes, indicating thatched roofs designed to protect against harsh winters.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e0f52198-46c5-49f5-9136-4f9c15213cba",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Material Culture: Inhabitants produced coarse gray, black, or reddish-brown handmade pottery. Tools were fashioned from polished stones and animal bones.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "20dc938e-337c-4918-bad7-eec17f0e1eca",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Burial Practices: Burials uncovered at the site show that red ochre was smeared on human skeletons before interment. Domesticated animals (such as dogs and wolves) were also buried alongside their masters.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "bc83373f-df29-4fab-8b4f-cfc1eec8f80b",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Agriculture: Paleo-botanical analysis indicates early cultivation of wheat, barley, and various types of lentils alongside wild plant gathering.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "1cfe5749-4b89-4953-879f-4775c73ba756",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Mahabharata Period",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b4bcb2d2-3fd0-424c-8f04-3b57431436bc",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The earliest dynastic memory of Kashmir is linked to the epic Mahabharata.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5f37d1cd-05be-4222-9361-f7a254c5eea5",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "The Kambojas: Ancient texts indicate that the Kamboja tribe ruled the region with their republican system of government centered at Rajapura (modern Rajouri).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "749434df-8576-4b84-b866-23ee3bda3570",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "The Panchalas: Later, the Panchalas established their influence over the area. The name Peer Panjal is widely considered a linguistic evolution of the ancient Sanskrit tribal term Panchala.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "df6388eb-8322-45e7-a798-94d3c139e10a",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Gonandic Dynasty: Kalhana begins the historical record of Rajatarangini just before the Mahabharata War. The first king mentioned is Gonanda I, who was killed in battle at Mathura. At the outbreak of the war, his infant successor Gonanda II was ruling Kashmir.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b4b32e27-be18-480a-87d6-837a35be6783",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "The Lost Kings: Kalhana records that the histories of 35 early kings were lost. However, the 19th-century historian Peerzada Ghulam Hassan recovered details of these rulers from a Persian manuscript written by Mulla Ahmad, who had translated an older, lost Sanskrit work called Ratnakar.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "9859e2f3-d584-4578-b462-3337d9d6945e",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "4. ANCIENT DYNASTIES AND EMPIRES",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d6ee030f-09a2-4cb1-a206-46d3bbcdec0d",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Mauryan Empire (c. 322 BC – 185 BC)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "38f9b041-4831-43ff-abe2-d4bd45d0187d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Mauryan hegemony was established over Jammu and Kashmir in the 3rd century BC under Emperor Ashoka.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "988f168a-8e42-4ec1-b692-8b9211c66cd2",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "[Majjhantika's Mission] ──> Deputed by Ashoka ──> Preached Buddhism in Kashmir ──> 500 Monks Arrive",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4d4951da-8167-492c-8602-1650ef35e376",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Srinagar (Pandrethan): Ashoka founded the original city of Srinagar, known as Puranadhisthana (located at modern-day Pandrethan).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "91dec6c6-fb14-43f6-9ac5-caecd3e88ef8",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Religious Patronage: Although a patron of Buddhism, Ashoka built several Viharas and also patronized local Shaivism, building a grand Shiva temple at Bijbehara (ancient Vijeshwari).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "903fd639-1e91-4733-8612-2b5535cd49bf",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Succession: After Ashoka’s death, his son Jaluka ascended the throne. Jaluka cleared the valley of foreign invader tribes (Mlechhas) and was succeeded by his son, Damodara II.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "37ecb6ef-6409-452f-b668-61467357d754",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Kushan Empire",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4e3499a5-ab6e-4a08-a9b8-58ae9595fea8",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Kalhana’s Rajatarangini details the occupation of the valley by three Turushka (Kushan) kings: Hushka, Jushka, and Kanishka.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "93851000-b304-4cdf-bc72-207db12fc5fe",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Town Foundations: Each king founded a town named after himself: Hushkapura (Ushkur, Baramulla), Jushkapura (Zukur, Srinagar), and Kanishkapura (Kanispora, Baramulla).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6b4ae37e-4f2a-47a3-854e-e96265e562d5",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> The Fourth Buddhist Council (c. 1st Century AD)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c96f7f33-a1a2-4a04-8163-4342d26ed785",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> Held under the patronage of Emperor Kanishka at Kundalvan (identified as Harwan near Shalimar Garden, Srinagar).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "805ca99e-386a-4055-93a3-9daf24dbca01",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> * Presidency: Presided over by the Kashmiri scholar Vasumitra, with Ashvaghosh serving as vice-president.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c6263e77-061d-4e64-9369-4961d877f944",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> * Significance: Attended by 500 Buddhist and Hindu scholars (including Nagarjuna and Vasubandhu). The council finalized the separation of Buddhism into the Hinayana and Mahayana sects.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b69ecc29-fcae-4c23-90e2-872893c7e95e",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Karkota Dynasty (c. AD 625 – 855)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7468781f-3347-4671-98bf-13fcb5c43b5b",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Founded by Durlabhavardhana (AD 625–661), the Karkota dynasty (also known as the Nagas) turned Kashmir into a major regional power.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "c389df5e-9049-43fe-9ab4-a73867202f72",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Foreign Visits: Both Chinese pilgrims Hiuen Tsang and Ou-Kong visited Kashmir during this dynasty. Hiuen Tsang spent two years (AD 631–633) studying Sanskrit scriptures, entering through the stone gate at Baramulla.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ae5cdddb-0129-4190-a1a9-850ba24f567a",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Lalitaditya Muktapida (AD 724–761): Known as the \"Samudra Gupta of Kashmir,\" Lalitaditya was a military genius. He launched successful military campaigns across Asia and India, conquering Punjab, Kannauj, Tibet, Ladakh, Bihar, Bengal, Gujarat, and parts of Southern India. He also repelled the Arab forces in Sindh.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8923d808-afa0-4507-9274-f2a5525a4b1f",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Martand Sun Temple: Built by Lalitaditya on the Mattan Karewa, this temple is a masterpiece of early medieval temple architecture. He also built a grand capital called Parihaspur (City of Pleasure) near the Kheer Bhawani shrine.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a504ca84-15bc-4c96-bea7-90e60e51c878",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Jayapida: The grandson of Lalitaditya, Jayapida (Vinayaditya), was the last prominent ruler of this dynasty, known for his patronage of literature and arts.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,

    },

    },
    {
      "id": "33edfd44-cbee-4b65-8b70-c024cfbee726",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Jayapida (Last powerful ruler; patron of letters)",
      "isBold": false,

      "highlightColorHex": "",

    },
    {
      "id": "bc81ee3a-72cb-4d38-b8f2-09059f7b9fab",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "5. MEDIEVAL PERIOD AND DYNASTIES",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f335aeba-9bae-4e2f-8a9d-96ea973cd8e4",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Utpala Dynasty (c. AD 855 – 939)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8423451d-8e9c-4df6-8ff3-266533272431",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "In AD 855, the Karkota dynasty was succeeded by the Utpala dynasty, founded by Avantivarman.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a00083b0-d864-432d-bdb9-32b60fdf210b",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Avantivarman (AD 855–883): Brought an era of peace, stability, and agricultural recovery. He founded the capital Avantipur and built two majestic temples: Avantisvara (dedicated to Shiva) and Avantisvamin (dedicated to Vishnu).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4d118ed8-899d-44d8-a5b6-47176dfc6c8c",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Suyya’s Engineering Feats: Avantivarman’s chief engineer, Suyya, engineered a massive flood-control scheme. He regulated the course of the Jhelum river, cleared silt blockages at the mouth of the Wular Lake, and reclaimed large tracts of swampy land for agriculture. He founded the town of Suyyapura (modern Sopore).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a7670a5f-722f-422a-9bfb-f3ae5eca53ca",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Shankarvarman (AD 883–902): Succeeded Avantivarman, marking the start of the dynasty's decline. He founded Shankarpura (modern Pattan). To finance his military campaigns, he imposed heavy taxes and introduced the system of Begar (forced labor).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "952aee6a-32c5-4637-a8b9-bd3e015c1fe6",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Gupta Dynasty (c. AD 948 – 1003)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d786b2cd-137d-4902-9348-4c79823a9e94",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Gupta Dynasty was founded by Parva Gupta. His son Kshemgupta ascended the throne in AD 950.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8698ec22-a5d8-4166-be69-ad8761d631b0",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Queen Didda: Kshemgupta married Princess Didda, the daughter of the King of Lohara (Poonch) and granddaughter of the Hindu Shahi King of Kabul. A highly ambitious, intelligent, and forceful figure, Didda ruled through puppet kings before formally ascending the throne in AD 980. She built several temples and monasteries.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a7004505-4cd9-470c-98dc-2d2e75ede488",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> Invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5a6c992a-1a4f-4ba2-9fab-a3be71d43ffc",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "> During Queen Didda's era, Mahmud of Ghazni twice attempted to invade and capture Kashmir. Both times, his forces were stopped by the impregnable defenses of the Loharakot Fort (located in modern Poonch), forcing him to retreat.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7ff30834-30a1-4303-82cc-5ef6b6c846a8",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Lohara Dynasty (c. AD 1003 – 1171)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f86b9934-894a-4d9f-8771-6b3ef9f88b5f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Founded by Sangramraj (Queen Didda's nephew) after her death in AD 1003.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "554f18dd-7750-4905-a856-18d7b6508b67",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "King Harsha (AD 1089–1101): An eccentric, highly cultured ruler who was also a patron of arts, but whose heavy taxation and destruction of temple idols for gold earned him the title of an iconoclast in his later years.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6d72d345-8d86-47f2-a68d-dbe69551deb7",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "King Jaisimha (AD 1128–1155): The last great ruler of the Hindu period. It was during his reign that Kalhana completed the Rajatarangini. The dynasty ended with the rule of Vanitadeva in AD 1171.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d6da1f57-25d5-4eeb-9207-beae369f781a",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Deva Dynasty and Mongol Invasion (c. AD 1171 – 1339)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "615026f2-e45b-4a8b-9ef7-032de5e390be",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Deva dynasty ruled Kashmir until the final collapse of Hindu political power in the early 14th century.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e50e7187-58a0-4298-84ba-8027dd3fc611",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Dulucha’s Invasion: During the reign of King Sahdev, a ruthless Mongol commander named Dulucha (or Zulju) invaded Kashmir through the Zoji La pass with a cavalry of 60,000 men. Dulucha pillaged the valley, slaughtered the male population, and enslaved thousands. Sahdev fled to Kishtwar, leaving the administrative apparatus in collapse.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a7d51d7e-829b-4839-aa5b-8c70a450ea57",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "The Three Adventurers: Sahdev's reign saw the arrival of three foreign adventurers who shaped Kashmir's history:",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "53589c60-2e47-4597-b86e-87f0ae181571",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Shah Mir (from Swat, Pakistan)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7382ab43-9cf7-4e01-8e2f-eacf4c89b55a",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Rinchen (a Buddhist prince from Ladakh)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "0b4bd4b0-be6e-457f-9bd4-cb318913f38d",
      "type": "NUMBERED_LIST",
      "text": "Lankar Chak (a Dard chief from Gilgit)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "71f7a696-87c7-4a90-8424-095f867b3beb",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Rinchen's Rule: Following Dulucha's withdrawal, Rinchen seized the throne and ruled for three years (AD 1320–1323). He converted to Islam under the influence of the Sufi saint Sayyid Sharf-ud-din (popularly known as Bulbul Shah), adopting the name Sultan Sadr-ud-din. He was Kashmir's first Muslim ruler.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "144acb4c-0786-4716-841d-39927bffeab4",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "6. MUSLIM RULE IN KASHMIR",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "5f6cfc3f-7b8e-4921-971c-5897aeb5f8af",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Shah Miri Dynasty (c. AD 1339 – 1561)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "0a553c41-c38e-45bc-81b3-c2c6bc75965d",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Following the death of Queen Kota Deva (the last Hindu ruler), Shah Mir ascended the throne in AD 1339 under the name Sultan Shams-ud-din, founding the Shah Miri Dynasty.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "3e4c4a4d-4a42-4918-af94-fde74cec9c94",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Sultan Shihab-ud-din (AD 1354–1373): Often called the \"Lalitaditya of Medieval Kashmir,\" he was a capable military general. He expanded the boundaries of Kashmir to include Kabul, Gilgit, Baltistan, Ladakh, and Kishtwar. He fought Feroz Shah Tughlaq on the banks of the Sutlej River, leading to a treaty that recognized Kashmarian authority over territories from Sindh to Kashmir. He founded Shihab-ud-din-pura (modern Shadipur).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6dfafb96-4867-4203-affc-4884d52346ca",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Sultan Sikandar (AD 1389–1413): Popularly referred to by some chroniclers as the \"Aurangzeb of Kashmir.\" He banned social customs like the Sati system and music. During his reign, Central Asian invader Taimur (Timur) sent envoys to Kashmir, presenting Sikandar with a wooden elephant as a diplomatic gift.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "bec6793a-9a4c-4809-8458-17f069c33d4d",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Sufi Missions: During the reign of Sultan Qutb-ud-din, the celebrated Sufi saint Mir Sayyid Ali Hamdani (Shah-i-Hamdan) arrived in Kashmir with 700 Syeds from Hamdan, Iran. This mission introduced Islamic jurisprudence, central Asian crafts, and the weaving of Kani shawls.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7f53c192-b33d-4013-a04d-197a67910a2b",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "[SULTAN ZAIN-UL-ABIDIN (\"BUDSHAH\")]",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ad548f2c-f21b-4f7d-8f0a-c52535c3ca42",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "a127ac69-61e9-44fe-a986-b30e8bc5df7f",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Socio-Economic Reforms Patronage & Culture",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b46fea6a-667a-4db1-aee5-3b191f5a4734",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Recalled exiled Pandits - Biographies: Zain Prakashan & Zain Charit",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "fa5851f0-0cf5-4cfe-9850-614ebf379171",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Abolished Jaziya & Sati ban - Introduced Paper Mache from Samarkand",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "85ee8a01-e090-4af8-bf37-a1c5ae2b61aa",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Built Zainakadal (1st wooden bridge) - Jonaraja wrote Dvitiya Rajatarangini",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b5b41f9e-37f4-486e-b7d5-4d6f67288003",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (AD 1420–1470): Affectionately called \"Budshah\" (The Great King).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "497bdb7a-1c91-4da2-9823-549b10a4b940",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Social & Religious Reforms: He initiated an era of religious harmony. He recalled Kashmiri Pandits who had fled, allowed forcibly converted Hindus to return to their faith, banned cow slaughter, rebuilt damaged temples, and abolished the Jaziya tax.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8495e011-8ae7-421b-aa2c-63fd57d1e7d3",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Art and Craft: He introduced the art of Paper Mache and silk weaving, bringing master craftsmen from Samarkand.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "4e0b7801-7de8-4469-9928-4276fa291c43",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Public Works: He founded the towns of Nowshahr, Zainapur, Zainakot, and Zainagir. He also built Zainakadal, the first wooden bridge in Srinagar.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "25ce0ebd-af28-4dee-846a-d9083c6dadce",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Biographies: His life was documented in two major contemporary works: Zain Prakashan by Yodh Bhatt and Zain Charit by Pandit Nathuram.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "6c557e91-408d-4128-80eb-2b25cc396c2b",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Chak Dynasty (AD 1561–1587)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f4730544-1103-4056-a17c-e54de8e7d9b7",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "The Shah Miri dynasty ended when Gazi Chak (a descendant of Lankar Chak) deposed Sultan Habib Shah. The Chaks were originally Dardic warriors from the Gilgit-Hunza region.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ad7fffc9-7da1-4fd0-84b6-69751ec1397b",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Mughal Defiance: The Chaks repeatedly repulsed annexation attempts by the Mughal Emperors Babur and Humayun.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "fa3c144e-4b9b-4e30-9dcb-50d140638146",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Yusuf Shah Chak: A patron of arts who married the legendary peasant-poetess Habba Khatoon (known as the Nightingale of Kashmir). He developed Gulmarg and Sonamarg into health resorts. He was eventually lured into negotiations, arrested by Akbar's general Qasim Khan at Haripura, and imprisoned in Bihar where he died. This paved the way for Mughal annexation in AD 1587.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e4f7e4ae-7198-414f-b225-089d8298ee46",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "7. THE MUGHAL, AFGHAN, AND SIKH PERIODS",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "8abbfb0a-dc29-43ab-8f8f-a6cc99d53f7b",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Mughal Dynasty (AD 1586 – 1751)",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "077882c2-adbc-4a8e-af60-9762259cd5ed",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Following the capture of Yusuf Shah Chak, Akbar integrated Kashmir into the Kabul Subah of the Mughal Empire.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d2adf825-f947-4d74-acad-b662f3ed791b",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Emperor Akbar: Visited Kashmir three times. His finance minister, Raja Todar Mal, carried out a comprehensive land revenue settlement. Akbar built the fortified town of Nagar-Magar around the Hari Parbat hill and constructed its outer stone wall (Kalai).",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "b8022d93-43cb-4ef6-8aee-02a4580f9e76",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Emperor Jahangir: Deeply enamored by the valley's beauty, he visited frequently and laid out the world-famous gardens of Shalimar, Nishat, Achabal, and Verinag.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "f1d3d6f3-044e-432e-8ecb-457b2599f71c",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Emperor Shah Jahan: Developed the Chashma Shahi garden and expanded Jahang",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    }
  ]
}

{
  "chapterId": "chap_9097b823",
  "title": "Pronouns",
  "elements": [
    {
      "id": "b18b28c4-3053-454b-adbf-c57436854d11",
      "type": "HEADING_1",
      "text": "PRONOUNS",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "69f60726-a16d-4342-bc75-bdf8bc2c6d5f",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "1. Introduction to Pronouns",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "ee8fc961-2dc3-427a-8735-0483d746145a",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "A Pronoun is a word used in place of a noun or noun phrase to avoid unnecessary repetition and make sentences clear, natural, and less awkward.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "e4cfd7f1-1a3e-4639-ae61-ad9d3a26baa9",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Example of Pronoun Usage",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "1a5578cb-4ab2-4661-aea1-02413f3a8ba1",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Repetitive: Rahul bought a car because Rahul likes cars.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "91030ed9-571e-440c-8404-14f0483d6e74",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Improved: Rahul bought a car because he likes them.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "d7ce392a-b705-49dc-87ec-90bd59bcbbe6",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Here, 'he' replaces 'Rahul' and 'them' replaces 'cars'. A pronoun therefore acts as a substitute for a noun.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "668fb1b9-a9dd-48ee-984c-3626666e8b59",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "Functions of Pronouns",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "3e805ae3-465a-48be-aa3e-5816693c1369",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "A pronoun can perform the same grammatical functions that a noun can perform, such as:",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {

    {
      "id": "d90bae4d-960a-45c3-b0c3-1856db7aa52b",

    {
      "id": "090feadb-41ff-4132-ba2c-6b6820747827",

    {
      "id": "d6ee11e2-1edb-4bb1-9e47-e81676e9defe",

      "text": "Interrogative Pronoun",
      "isBold": false,

      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "391058ec-d07b-41a5-a1fb-b45a97a04818",
      "type": "HEADING_2",
      "text": "2. Personal Pronoun",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "7326372f-dc7d-47e9-91cc-4f588ece7838",
      "type": "PARAGRAPH",
      "text": "Personal Pronouns are pronouns used to represent specific people, animals, or things. They change their form according to Person, Number, Gender, and Case.",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "73632c8b-08cb-463d-993b-035e28f39e73",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "The Three Grammatical Persons",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "81177cfb-cd33-4b01-899a-71f5a7c86c8d",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "First Person (The person speaking): Singular -> I, Plural -> We",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "dc4a2daf-8a5d-472c-bc93-5c50772539e2",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Second Person (The person spoken to): Singular\/Plural -> You",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "df4d6deb-deb8-4b75-a17f-c48eef270cbe",
      "type": "BULLET_LIST",
      "text": "Third Person (The person, animal, or thing spoken about): Masculine singular -> He, Feminine singular -> She, Neuter singular -> It, Plural -> They",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "64efedae-d9b1-4dda-a23a-47c3f646781b",
      "type": "HEADING_3",
      "text": "Cases of Personal Pronouns",
      "isBold": false,
      "isItalic": false,
      "isUnderline": false,
      "isStrikethrough": false,
      "textColorHex": "",
      "highlightColorHex": "",
      "alignment": "LEFT"
    },
    {
      "id": "832ae810-3c5f-4b19-9eb5-99d35c61567c",
      "type": "TABLE",
      "title": "Personal Pronoun Cases Grid",
      "headers": [
        "Person",
        "Subjective \/ Nominative",
        "Objective",
        "Possessive Pronoun",
        "Possessive Adjective"
      ],
      "rows": [
        [
          "1st Singular",
          "I",
          "Me",
          "Mine",
          "My"
        ],
        [
          "1st Plural",
          "We",
          "Us",
          "Ours",
          "Our"
        ],
        [
          "2nd Singular\/Plural",
          "You",
          "You",
          "Yours",
          "Your"
        ],
        [
          "3rd Singular Masculine",
          "He",

          "His",
          "His"
        ],
        [
          "3rd Singular Feminine",
          "She",
          "Her",
          "Hers",
          "Her"
        ],
        [
          "3rd Singular Neuter",
          "It",
          "It",
          "—",
          "Its"
        ],
        [
          "3rd Plural",
